title: Chapter 4 Quiz: Computed Properties & Watchers
description: Test your knowledge of computed properties, watchers, and their use cases.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using a computed property over a method in the template?
options: Computed properties are cached based on dependencies
Computed properties are easier to write
questions.explanation: Computed properties cache their results and only recompute when dependencies change, which improves performance and prevents unnecessary recalculations.

questions.question: Computed properties are re-evaluated every time the component re-renders.
questions.explanation: No, computed properties are only re-evaluated when one of their reactive dependencies changes, not on every render.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid use case for a watcher?
options: Filtering a list based on user input
Making an API call when a search query changes
questions.explanation: Watchers are ideal for side effects like API calls. Formatting, filtering, and concatenation are better handled by computed properties.

questions.question: To make a computed property writable, you define it as an object with a __________ and a setter.
questions.explanation: A writable computed property uses an object with a `get` function and a `set` function.

questions.question: Watchers can be used to watch computed properties as well as data properties.
questions.explanation: Yes, watchers can observe any reactive property, including computed properties.

questions.question: What does the `immediate: true` option do in a watcher?
options: Runs the watcher handler immediately after the component is created
Causes the watcher to run synchronously
Prevents the watcher from running on the first change
Makes the watcher run only once
questions.explanation: `immediate: true` runs the watcher handler once during component creation, before any changes.

questions.question: To watch for changes inside a nested object, you need to set the __________ option to true.
questions.explanation: The `deep: true` option enables deep watching of nested properties.

questions.question: Computed properties can accept arguments.
questions.explanation: Computed properties are functions that take no arguments. If you need to pass arguments, use a method instead.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid way to define a watcher?
questions.explanation: Watcher handlers cannot be arrow functions because they need to access the component instance via `this`. Arrow functions do not bind their own `this`.

questions.question: What happens if you use a computed property that depends on an array, and you modify the array by pushing a new item?
options: The computed property will not update because the array reference didn't change
The computed property will update because Vue tracks array mutations
You must manually call a method to recompute
The computed property will only update if you reassign the array
questions.explanation: Vue's reactivity system can detect array mutations like `push`, `pop`, `splice`, etc., so the computed property will recalc.

questions.question: Watchers are automatically cleaned up when the component is destroyed.
questions.explanation: Yes, Vue automatically stops watchers when the component is destroyed.

questions.question: The function inside a computed property is called a __________.
questions.explanation: A computed property defines a getter function that returns the computed value.

questions.question: Which of the following is a good use case for a computed property with a setter?
options: Updating a first name and last name when a full name is set
Making an API call when a search term changes
Checking if a user is logged in
questions.explanation: A setter is useful when you want to update multiple data properties from a single computed property assignment, like splitting a full name into first and last.

questions.question: You can use `v-model` with a computed property that has a setter.
questions.explanation: Yes, `v-model` works with writable computed properties, as it calls the setter when the input changes.

questions.question: How can you watch multiple data properties with a single handler?
options: Use a computed property that combines them and watch that
Use a watcher with the `deep` option on an object containing them
Use an array of property names in the watcher
Both A and B are valid approaches
questions.explanation: You can either create a computed property that returns an object with the values and watch it with `deep`, or put them together in a reactive object and watch that object with `deep`.

questions.question: To watch a property with the name 'user.name', you need to wrap it in __________ when defining the watcher key.
questions.explanation: Because of the dot, you need to write it as a string: `watch: { 'user.name'(newVal) { ... } }`.

questions.question: A computed property can return a Promise.
questions.explanation: Computed properties are synchronous by design. For async operations, use watchers or methods.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a computed property and a watcher?
options: Computed properties are for side effects; watchers are for derived data
Computed properties are for derived data with caching; watchers are for side effects
Computed properties can be async; watchers cannot
There is no difference; they are interchangeable
questions.explanation: Computed properties are for deriving new data with caching, while watchers are for performing side effects when data changes.

questions.question: The two arguments passed to a watcher handler are the __________ and the __________.
questions.explanation: Watcher handlers receive the new value as the first argument and the old value as the second argument.

questions.question: Deep watchers can cause performance issues if used on large objects.
questions.explanation: Deep watchers traverse the entire object recursively, which can be expensive. Use them judiciously.
